headline: State desk: South Dakota panel faces cut; Portland weighs drive-thrus
dek: South Dakota's medical cannabis oversight chair wants her own committee scrapped as patients top 20,185, and Portland may let dispensaries sell through drive-thru windows.
key_points: Rep. Josephine Garcia, chair of South Dakota's Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee, told the Legislature's Executive Board on 10 November that the panel should be eliminated; the board accepted its report but took no action.
South Dakota had 20,185 registered medical cannabis patients in October, and the committee made no recommendations in 2026 after 11 in 2025.
Portland Mayor Keith Wilson's Ordinance 2026-407 would drop the city's ban on dispensary drive-thru and walk-up windows, which state rules have allowed since 2020.
The same ordinance would raise the down payment for deferred licence fees from $500 to half the $3,970 annual fee; the council returns to it on 8 December.
body: Two local stories from the past 48 hours show how much cannabis regulation is still being shaped in committee rooms rather than at the ballot box. In South Dakota, the chair of the legislative panel that oversees the medical cannabis program has recommended doing away with it. In Portland, Oregon, the mayor wants to scrap a decade-old ban on selling cannabis through drive-thru and walk-up windows, and tighten how dispensaries pay their city licence fees.
## South Dakota: an oversight panel with nothing to recommend

Rep. Josephine Garcia, the Watertown Republican who chairs South Dakota's Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee, told the Legislature's Executive Board on Tuesday, 10 November, that the committee has largely done its job and should be eliminated, The Marijuana Herald and KCCR reported. She suggested that the departments of Health, Revenue and Agriculture, along with medical professionals, could carry on the discussion instead, and said that if the committee survives, a pharmacist should be added to it. Her recommendation is not an official committee position.

Not everyone agreed. Republican Sen. Tom Pischke asked how lawmakers would get recommendations on the program without the committee and floated changing its membership and duties instead. The board accepted the committee's annual report but took no action on dissolving it.

The panel was created after voters approved Initiated Measure 26 in 2020, and state law gives it a broad remit: patient access, dispensaries, cultivation, testing, safeguards and research. In 2026 it met twice, on 17 August and 13 October, heard presentations on federal rescheduling and other topics, and adopted no recommendations. That is a sharp drop from 2025, when its final report carried 11 recommendations on matters including THC potency limits, facility inspections and police access to patient information.

The committee has had a contentious year. At its October meeting, industry advocates accused it of stacking agendas with critics of medical cannabis from outside the state, South Dakota Searchlight reported. Garcia and co-chair Sen. John Carley both lost their primary races in June, so the panel's leadership will change regardless.

Lawmakers have tried this before. House Bill 1160, which would have repealed the committee, passed the House 41-26 in February but failed in the Senate 15-19 in March. Ending or reshaping it would require a change in state law, and the next session opens on 12 January 2027.

Meanwhile the program keeps growing. The Department of Health counted 20,185 registered patients in October, with 673 caregivers and 223 providers. In August the count was 19,821, so the program has added more than 360 patients in two months.
> South Dakota's medical program keeps adding patients while the panel meant to watch it struggles to agree on anything to say.
## Portland: catching up with the state on drive-thrus

In Portland, Mayor Keith Wilson has introduced Ordinance 2026-407, which would amend Chapter 14B.130 of the city code, the chapter that governs cannabis business licences. The City Life Committee took it up on 10 November without a vote and listed it as continued to 8 December, according to the city's council records and local reporting.

The headline change removes language that bars cannabis retailers from selling through drive-thru facilities or walk-up windows. The city's ban mirrored state rules when it was written in 2015. But in March 2020 the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission allowed curbside pickup and delivery within 150 feet of a store, including through existing windows, and made that permanent in September 2020. Portland's code never followed. The change would apply only to windows already built into a lawfully permitted building; sales from carts, temporary structures and satellite sites would stay banned, and store hours would remain limited to 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.

The second change matters more to many operators' cash flow. Portland's annual cannabis licence fee is $3,970, and about 31% of licensees use the city's deferred payment programme. City staff told the committee they have found significant misuse, with many licensees missing the balance after the deferral period. The ordinance would raise the required down payment from $500 to 50% of the annual fee, $1,985 at today's rate, with the rest due within six months. Late fees would start at 14 days instead of 30, and a second late fee at 60 days would be dropped. Fixed fee amounts would come out of the code so future changes can be made through the budget.

In South Dakota, watch for a bill to repeal or restructure the oversight committee when the session opens on 12 January. In Portland, the council's City Life Committee returns to the ordinance on 8 December, with public testimony open until then, and KXL reported the council is expected to vote on it next month.
